Mitochondrial dysfunction in aortic disease pathogenesis

Mitochondrial dysfunction in aortic disease pathogenesis. This schematic highlights mitochondrial metabolic alterations implicated in the development of aortic aneurysm and dissection (AAD). (a) TCA cycle metabolic reprogramming. This panel illustrates disruptions in the TCA cycle contributing to AAD progression, integrating mechanisms from three key studies. Pathways are color-coded for clarity: Blue represents the NR1D1-ACO2 axis, in which the nuclear receptor NR1D1 targets mitochondrial ACO2 to regulate TCA cycle flux and abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) development. Red highlights succinate accumulation as a biomarker and therapeutic target that drives AAD’s inflammation, oxidative stress, and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation. Orange depicts ANK deficiency-mediated cytosolic citrate buildup, which promotes histone acetylation, CCL2/IL-6 expression, and MMP activation, exacerbating aortic aneurysm formation. (b) Electron transport chain (ETC) dysfunction. This panel depicts mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) impairments in aortic cells, drawing from three seminal studies on aortic disease. Downregulation of nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) leads to NAD+ depletion, impairing OXPHOS in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), promoting cell senescence, DNA damage, and synthetic phenotype switching. NAMPT-enriched extracellular vesicles from mesenchymal stem cells restore NAMPT levels and mitigate AAA. CD36 signaling in macrophages, triggered by oxidized LDL, shifts mitochondrial metabolism from OXPHOS to superoxide production, upregulating fatty acid uptake, downregulating fatty acid oxidation (FAO), and activating NFκB for inflammatory cytokine release. TNF signaling dampens OXPHOS by enhancing AP-1 transcriptional activity, which drives VSMC degenerative programs. CoQ10 or AP-1 inhibitors rescue OXPHOS and improve survival. (c) Dysregulated lipid metabolism and mitochondrial injury. This panel summarizes dysregulated lipid pathways in vascular cells during AAA and atherosclerosis. PKM2 in T lymphocytes drives EV release enriched in polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and phospholipids, inducing macrophage iron accumulation, lipid peroxidation, migration, and AAA. Triglycerides inhibit lysyl oxidase (LOX) maturation and reduce LOX activity, and hypertriglyceridemia is a key contributor to AAA pathogenesis. Platelet ACER1 deficiency elevates ceramides, activating p38 MAPK to promote pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion; ACER1-mediated ceramide catabolism mitigates inflammation and AAA. Long-chain ceramides act as endogenous ligands for the G protein-coupled receptors CYSLTR2 and P2RY6 on endothelial cells and macrophages. This direct receptor activation triggers Gq signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, aggravating plaque inflammation independently of cholesterol levels. Endothelial soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) upregulation metabolizes PUFAs to diols, disrupting mitochondrial protein-cholesterol associations, inhibiting complex I, elevating ROS, reducing membrane potential, activating TGFβ, and promoting atherosclerosis progression.
